improvement_notes: The lesson is technically strong but unusually long for a foundational electricity class. Consolidate repeated warnings about meter configuration, datasheets, supervision, and model limitations so the central learning progression remains visible.

Add a short explicit distinction between electrical energy and battery capacity: watt-hours describe stored energy approximately under stated conditions, while ampere-hours alone do not specify energy without voltage.

The H-bridge section is accurate but dense for beginners. Introduce the motor-driver purpose with a two-output conceptual sketch first, then reveal the four-switch bridge and shoot-through explanation.
The Python lab is well aligned with the resistor model, but learners would benefit from one guided prediction prompt immediately before execution and a brief sample output block for offline learners.
Clarify in the measurement activity that students should not independently move meter leads or reconfigure current mode; the instructor should perform or directly supervise those actions.

The generated diagrams are useful, but the generic diagram.png instruction to trace ideas from left to right is less specific than the surrounding visuals. Give it a precise caption and one or two learner questions tied to its labeled elements.
Use a real, carefully staged low-voltage robot-electronics photograph to connect the abstractions to physical battery, driver, motor, return wiring, and measurement equipment.

linkedin.title: Class 6: Electricity for Roboticists—From Voltage and Current to Motor Drivers
linkedin.description: A rigorous Professor OS lesson connects voltage, current, resistance, power, LED sizing, H-bridges, meter safety, and motor behavior through calculations and a Python lab.
linkedin.commentary:
Robots do not move because “electricity” is mysterious. They move because a source, circuit, driver, and motor transfer energy through a complete and measurable path.

In Class 6, Professor OS helps learners build that model step by step:

• Use voltage, current, and resistance without overextending the water-pipe analogy.
• Apply Ohm’s law and power equations with units and sanity checks.
• Size a resistor for an LED indicator under realistic supply variation.
• Understand why motor startup and stall current differ from normal operation.
• Practice safer multimeter reasoning and connect simplified calculations to an H-bridge.

The included Python lab reinforces the resistor model, while the RoboRover challenge asks students to predict outcomes before checking them. Try the simulation first, then complete the low-voltage measurement activity only with appropriate supervision and current-limited equipment.
